notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on **1 Samuel 2**, drawn from the sites and traditions you specified. I could retrieve material from Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic), BibleHub (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit), Precept Austin (evangelical, with Wiersbe, MacArthur, Bergen), DesiringGod (Reformed Baptist), and GTY (Reformed Baptist). I was unable to fetch Catholic/Orthodox, Lutheran, Methodist, or modern‑scholarship pages — those gaps are noted below.

---

## Hannah’s Song (vv. 1–10)

**Overview.** Commentators across traditions agree that Hannah’s prayer is a prophetic hymn of thanksgiving — often called “the Magnificat of the Old Testament.” The Pulpit Commentary notes that Hannah’s hymn “begins with the temporal mercies accorded to herself, but rises immediately into the realms of prophecy, foretelling Christ’s kingdom.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_samuel/2.htm) Ellicott says Hannah “had learned by Divine revelation” that Samuel would be God’s instrument first to restore true religion, then to found a kingly order in Israel. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/2.htm) Dr. Constable (Dallas Seminary) observes that this prayer “provides the key to interpreting the rest of 1 and 2 Samuel,” since Hannah articulates the belief that “God rewards trust with blessing.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-2.html)

---

**v. 1 — “My heart rejoices in the LORD in whom my horn is exalted…”**

Gill notes that Hannah “had prayed before, but that was mental, this vocal; she had prayed and was answered… and now she gives thanks for it.” He adds that the Targum says she prayed “by a spirit of prophecy,” which is why the Jews reckon her one of the seven prophetesses. Gill emphasizes she rejoiced “not in her son… but in the goodness and kindness of the Lord.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/2.htm)

Enduring Word (David Guzik) stresses the context: Hannah offered this worship “on the very day she left her little boy — her only child — at the tabernacle, never for him to live in her home again.” Her joy is in the LORD, not in circumstances. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-2/)

Ellicott explains that “horn” is a favourite Hebrew symbol for strength (from oxen), and “mine horn is exalted” means “I am strong — mighty now in the gift I have received.” “My mouth is enlarged” means she can now speak boldly where before she was silenced by Peninnah’s taunts. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/2.htm)

Precept Austin, citing Wiersbe: “To have your ‘horn exalted’ meant to receive new strength from God and be especially helped by Him at a time of crisis.” It also notes the NET’s observation that “horn” alludes to an animal elevating its head in a display of strength. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-2-commentary)

---

**v. 2 — “There is no one holy like the LORD…”**

Gill expounds that God is “essentially, originally, independently, perfectly, and immutably holy, as others are not.” Even angels’ holiness is derived and imperfect by comparison. “There is none besides Thee” is “a primary philosophical truth… that outside of God is no existence” (Pulpit). The rock metaphor, first found in Deuteronomy 32:4, speaks of God’s “strength, calm, immovable, enduring” nature (Ellicott). Gill adds that “rock” points to Christ: “there is no rock like him for strength and duration; none like him for a foundation to build upon.” (All at https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/2.htm and https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/2.htm)

Precept Austin notes the Hebrew parallelism: the three lines of v. 2 all “rhyme” ideas, not sounds — a classic feature of Hebrew poetry. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-2-commentary)

---

**v. 3 — “Do not boast so proudly… for the LORD is a God who knows, and by Him actions are weighed.”**

Gill sees Hannah addressing Peninnah directly, warning her (and all the arrogant) to “talk no more so exceeding proudly.” He notes the Hebrew “God of knowledges” (plural intensive) means God has perfect knowledge of every proud word, thought, and deed. To “weigh” actions means God “examines them, whether they proceed from a right principle to a right end.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/2.htm)

Ellicott records a textual note: this is one of fifteen places where the Masorites indicate the Hebrew should read “by Him” (lo with vav) rather than “not” (lo with aleph). The sense is that God weighs all human actions according to their essential worth, taking all motives into account. The Talmud (Berachoth 33) comments that “knowledge is of great price, for it is placed between two Divine names.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/2.htm)

---

**v. 4 — “The bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble are equipped with strength.”**

Ellicott: “Every power which will be something in itself is destroyed by the Lord; every weakness which despairs of itself is transformed into power” (quoting Von Gerlach). The “bows of the heroes” is a poetic figure — the weapon is named instead of the warrior. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/2.htm)

Gill sees a spiritual application: “the bows of Satan… are broken, and his fiery darts are quenched,” while the weak in faith are “girded by the Lord with strength” to “exercise grace, perform duty… and persevere.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/2.htm)

---

**v. 5 — “The well-fed hire themselves out for food… the barren woman gives birth to seven…”**

Gill reads the “full” as those who were once wealthy but reduced to hiring themselves out for bread, and the “hungry” as those who now “ceased” from hunger — a picture of providential reversals. “The barren hath born seven” he applies to Hannah herself (she eventually had five more children besides Samuel — seven being “a number put for many”). The Jewish tradition (via Jarchi) holds that “when Hannah bore one child, Peninnah buried two.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/2.htm)

Ellicott adds that this verse contains “another image to illustrate the vicissitudes of human affairs,” with seven children representing the full number of divine blessing (cf. Ruth 4:15). He also notes the typical reference: “the long barrenness of the Gentile world, to be followed by a fruitfulness far exceeding that of the Jewish Church.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/2.htm)

---

**v. 6 — “The LORD brings death and gives life; He brings down to Sheol and raises up.”**

Gill interprets this both of physical death and resurrection and of spiritual death and regeneration: “The Lord kills by the law… and he makes alive by His Spirit, through the Gospel.” He cites the cases of Lazarus and the general resurrection. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/2.htm)

Ellicott: “Death too and life come from this same omnipotent Lord: nothing in the affairs of men is the sport of blind chance.” He quotes the Babylonian Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 16) which uses this verse to describe three classes at judgment — the perfectly righteous, the thoroughly wicked, and those in an intermediate state who “go down into hell… whence they ascend again.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/2.htm)

---

**v. 7 — “The LORD sends poverty and wealth; He humbles and He exalts.”**

Gill applies this naturally (e.g., Job) and spiritually: “it is He that makes men sensible of their poverty, and then makes them rich in spiritual things… which come to them through the poverty of Christ, who, though He was rich, became poor” (2 Cor 8:9). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/2.htm)

---

**v. 8 — “He raises the poor from the dust… to seat them among princes…”**

Gill sees the “poor” and “beggar” as spiritually poor sinners whom God finds in the “dust” and “dunghill” of sin, then raises to sit “among princes” — the people of God, “sons of the King of kings.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/2.htm)

Ellicott comments on “the pillars of the earth”: “The quiet thinker… is tempted to ask whether… now, with the light of modern science shining round us, we have made much real progress in our knowledge of the genesis and government of the universe.” Gesenius prefers “foundations”; the Vulgate (Jerome) renders it “hinges” (cardines terrae). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/2.htm)

---

**v. 9 — “He guards the steps of His faithful ones, but the wicked perish in darkness; for by his own strength shall no man prevail.”**

Ellicott calls this “the comforting deduction Hannah drew from the circumstances of her life.” The Talmud (Yoma 38) comments: “If any man has passed the greater part of his years without sin, he will sin no more… for it is said, ‘He will keep the feet of his saints.’” Ellicott compares the closing phrase to Zechariah 4:6 (“Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit”) and 2 Corinthians 12:9 (“My strength is made perfect in weakness”). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/2.htm)

---

**v. 10 — “Those who oppose the LORD will be shattered… He will give power to His king. He will exalt the horn of His anointed.”**

This is the **first use of “Messiah” (Anointed) in the Bible**. Ellicott notes the LXX renders it “Christou autou” (“His Christ”). Jewish expositors have generally interpreted these words as a prophecy of King Messiah. Ellicott: “The words received a partial fulfilment in the splendid reigns of David and Solomon; but the pious Jew looked on the golden halo… as but a pale reflection of the glory which would accompany King Messiah when He should appear.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/2.htm)

Enduring Word (Guzik): “This is the first place in the Bible where Jesus is referred to as the Messiah… Zecharias, the father of John the Baptist, quoted Hannah in Luke 1:69… Mary the mother of Jesus quoted Hannah’s song often (Luke 1:46-55).” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-2/)

Dr. Constable observes that both Hannah’s Song (1 Sam 2) and David’s Song (2 Sam 22) frame 1–2 Samuel as an inclusio: “Both begin by using ‘horn’… referring to God as the ‘Rock,’” and “both end by paralleling ‘his king’ with ‘his anointed.’” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-2.html)

---

## Samuel Ministers; Eli’s Wicked Sons (vv. 11–26)

**v. 11 — “Then Elkanah went home to Ramah, but the boy began ministering to the LORD before Eli the priest.”**

Ellicott: “The word ‘minister’ is the official term used to signify the duties performed by priests and Levites.” Enduring Word notes that “young as he was, Samuel had a ministry to the LORD” and that “our young people can praise and please God.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-2/; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/2.htm)

---

**v. 12 — “Now the sons of Eli were wicked men; they had no regard for the LORD.”**

Ellicott explains the Hebrew “sons of Belial” simply means “sons of worthlessness” — worthless, good-for-nothing men. “They knew not the LORD” means they were “utter unbelievers” who “used their sacred position merely as affording an opportunity for their selfish extortions.” Dean Stanley is quoted: “They are true exemplars of the grasping and worldly clergy of all ages.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/2.htm)

Enduring Word: “They did not know the LORD… that knowledge was not passed on genetically… they had to personally know the LORD for themselves.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-2/)

---

**vv. 13–14 — The three-pronged fork abuse.**

The Law (Lev 7:31–35; Deut 18:3) gave priests the breast and shoulder of peace offerings. But Eli’s sons introduced a “custom” — sending a servant with a three-pronged fork to take whatever it brought up from the boiling pot. Ellicott: “this was a graver offence… the modest share of the offerings assigned to them by the Law of Moses” was replaced by robbery. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/2.htm)

Enduring Word adds that this was some 400 years after Moses, and the priestly custom had corrupted into self-serving greed. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-2/)

---

**vv. 15–16 — Demanding raw meat before the fat was burned.**

The fat was God’s portion, to be burned first (Lev 3:16; 7:23–31). Taking meat before burning the fat was “a crime which was equivalent to robbing God” (Ellicott). The demand for raw meat (rather than boiled) may indicate they wanted to sell it — raw meat was easier to market (Enduring Word). The threat of violence (“I will take it by force”) shows “the greed of Eli’s sons was so bad that they did not hesitate to use violence” (Enduring Word). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/2.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-2/)

---

**v. 17 — “Thus the sin of these young men was severe… for they were treating the LORD’s offering with contempt.”**

Ellicott notes the Latin phrase “grave peccatum sacerdotum ob scandalum” — a grave sin of the priests because of the scandal. The worshippers “abhorred the offering of the LORD” — the priests made people hate coming to worship. Enduring Word: “It was bad enough what they themselves did, but the greater sin… was in how they hurt other people.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/2.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-2/)

---

**v. 18 — “Now Samuel was ministering before the LORD — a boy wearing a linen ephod.”**

The contrast is deliberate. Even as a child, Samuel “distinguished himself in his service to the LORD,” receiving a linen ephod, a priestly garment (Ex 39:27–29). Trapp is quoted by Enduring Word: “He did small charges, as setting up lights, laying up vestments, learning music, or the like.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-2/)

---

**vv. 19–21 — Hannah’s yearly robe; Eli’s blessing; Hannah’s five more children.**

“His mother used to make him a little robe” — Enduring Word notes that “only someone who was really there would describe such a small detail.” Though Hannah gave Samuel to God, “she never stopped loving him.” Eli’s blessing (“May the LORD give you children… in place of the one she dedicated”) is fulfilled: God gives Hannah three more sons and two daughters. Enduring Word: “God will never be a debtor to anyone.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-2/)

---

**v. 22 — “Now Eli was very old…” and his sons were sleeping with the women at the Tent of Meeting.**

Enduring Word: “This was an ancient version of the modern sex scandals among pastors.” The women who “assembled at the door” may have been workers at the sanctuary (cf. Ex 38:8). The narrative focus is shifting from the sons to Eli himself — he heard about everything but only rebuked. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-2/)

---

**vv. 23–25 — Eli’s ineffective rebuke.**

Eli said, “Why do you do such things? … If a man sins against another man, God can intercede for him; but if a man sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him?”

Enduring Word calls this “the worst thing a parent can do… just talk. All he did was whine… but he never took the necessary actions.” John Trapp (17th c.) is quoted suggesting what Eli *should* have said: “Draw near hither, ye sons of the sorceress… ye brats of fathomless perdition… It is stark stinking naught that I hear.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-2/)

Eli’s rhetorical question “who can intercede?” finds its answer in 1 John 2:1 — “we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (Enduring Word).

On **“the LORD intended to put them to death”** — Enduring Word explains: “God judged Eli’s sons this way: He gave them exactly what they wanted. They did not want to repent, and God did not work repentance in their hearts.” This is a matter of judicial hardening. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-2/)

**John Piper** (Reformed Baptist, DesiringGod) has preached on this passage in “When God’s Will Is That His Will Not Be Done” (based on 1 Sam 2:22–25). He addresses the tension between God’s revealed will (that all repent) and His sovereign decree (that some are hardened). (https://www.desiringgod.org/scripture/1-samuel — sermon listed; full content not retrievable.)

---

**v. 26 — “And the boy Samuel continued to grow in stature and in favor with the LORD and with man.”**

Enduring Word notes the deliberate contrast with Eli’s sons, and points out that though Eli was a flawed father, he “essentially fathered Samuel and he grew up to be a godly man.” The language anticipates Luke 2:52 about the boy Jesus. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-2/)

---

## The Man of God’s Judgment on Eli’s House (vv. 27–36)

**vv. 27–29 — The unnamed man of God confronts Eli.**

God reminds Eli: “Did I not clearly reveal Myself to your father’s house when they were in Egypt…?” The “father” is Aaron. Ellicott’s Excursus C traces the high priestly line from Eleazar (Aaron’s son) to Eli (of Ithamar’s line), suggesting the office transferred to Eli’s family when the Eleazar line had only an infant heir and Eli had distinguished himself in the wars of the judges’ period. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/2.htm)

Enduring Word explains the four priestly duties listed in v. 28: (1) to be God’s priest first, not the people’s; (2) to offer sacrifices; (3) to burn incense (picturing prayer); (4) to wear the ephod (representing God’s glory and beauty). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-2/)

The accusation in v. 29 — “You have honored your sons more than Me by fattening yourselves with the best” — strikes Eli for both failing to discipline his sons and benefiting from their theft. Enduring Word: “If Eli were more afraid of offending God and less afraid of offending his sons he would have corrected them as he should have.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-2/)

---

**v. 30 — “I will honor those who honor Me, but those who despise Me will be disdained.”**

Dr. Constable identifies this as the **key verse of 1–2 Samuel**: “Every section of 1 and 2 Samuel demonstrates the truth of this statement.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-2.html)

Enduring Word shares the story of Eric Liddell (the Olympic runner and missionary) who received a slip of paper with this verse before his 1924 400m race — which he won in world-record time. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-2/)

---

**vv. 31–33 — “I will cut off your strength… no older man… distress in My dwelling place… your eyes will fail…”**

“Cut off your arm” is figurative — the arm symbolizes strength in Hebrew thought. The judgment is that Eli’s house will lose the high priesthood and be marked by premature death and sorrow. Enduring Word: “All your descendants will die by the sword of men” — this was fulfilled when Saul slaughtered the priests at Nob (1 Sam 22) and when Solomon deposed Abiathar (1 Kings 2:26–27). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-2/)

---

**v. 34 — The sign: Hophni and Phinehas will both die on the same day.**

This is fulfilled in 1 Samuel 4:11 when both are killed in battle against the Philistines. Enduring Word: “Since the fulfillment of the judgment would be many years away (in the days of Solomon), God gave Eli an immediate sign to demonstrate His truthfulness.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-2/)

---

**v. 35 — “Then I will raise up for Myself a faithful priest…”**

Who is this “faithful priest”? Enduring Word (Guzik) gives a threefold answer: (1) **Samuel** — a partial fulfillment, acting as priest though a Levite; (2) **Zadok** — whose line replaced Abiathar/Eli’s line under Solomon (1 Kings 2:27, 35); (3) ultimately **Jesus Christ** — the eternal faithful priest who “will do whatever is in My heart and mind” and who has “an enduring house.” The phrase “he will walk before My anointed one for all time” points beyond any mortal priest to the Messiah. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-2/)

Ellicott agrees: “A Lapide, quoted by Wordsworth, wrote here, ‘haec omnia spectant ad Christum’ — all these things have regard to Christ.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/2.htm)

---

**v. 36 — “Everyone left in your house will come and bow down to him for a piece of silver…”**

Eli’s surviving descendants will be reduced to begging for the lowest priestly position just to eat. Enduring Word: This was ultimately fulfilled when Abiathar was deposed by Solomon and Zadok took his place. The once-proud priestly family of Eli would be reduced to poverty and dependence. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-2/)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

**Reformed / Baptist — Divine Sovereignty and Hardening (v. 25).** John Piper (DesiringGod, Reformed Baptist) preached on “When God’s Will Is That His Will Not Be Done” from 1 Sam 2:22–25, addressing the tension between God’s revealed will and His sovereign decree — that God “desired to kill them” means He actively withheld repentance. This reflects a Calvinist understanding of reprobation. (https://www.desiringgod.org/scripture/1-samuel) John MacArthur (GTY) also teaches from this passage, seeing Hannah as a model of godly motherhood and emphasizing God’s sovereignty in raising up Samuel amid corruption. (https://www.gty.org/sermons/1279/how-to-be-a-godly-mother)

**Pentecostal / Charismatic — Prophetic Song (vv. 1–10).** Enduring Word (David Guzik) emphasizes that Hannah’s song was Spirit‑inspired prophecy — she is the first person in Scripture to use the title “Messiah” (v. 10). Her experience illustrates that “true strength and vindication come from God, not from our circumstances.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-2/)

**Methodist / Wesleyan and Lutheran —** I was unable to retrieve pages from seedbed.com, 1517.org, or lcms.org due to search/fetch limits. No notes available from these traditions.
